             New York Journal of Mathematics
                           New York J. Math. 28 (2022) 494–522.


   Some braces of cardinality 𝒑𝟒 and related
           Hopf-Galois extensions
 D. Puljić, A. Smoktunowicz and K. Nejabati Zenouz

        Abstract. We describe all 𝔽𝑝 -braces of cardinality 𝑝4 which are not right
        nilpotent. The constructed braces are solvable and prime, and contain a non-
        zero strongly nilpotent ideal. We use the constructed braces to construct ex-
        amples of finitely dimensional pre-Lie algebras which are left nilpotent but
        not right nilpotent. We also explain some well known results about the cor-
        respondence between braces and Hopf-Galois extensions using the notion of
        Hopf-Galois extensions associated to a given brace. This can be applied to the
        constructed 𝔽𝑝 -braces.

1. Introduction
   In 2005, W. Rump introduced braces as a generalisation of Jacobson radical
rings in order to help study involutive set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter
equation. Since then braces have been studied solely for their algebraic prop-
erties and have been linked to other research areas. For example, T. Gateva-
Ivanova showed that braces are in correspondence with braided groups with an
involutive braiding operator in [10]. Braces have also been shown to be equiv-
alent to some objects in group theory such as bijective 1-cocycles and regular
  Received September 15, 2021.
  2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. 16W35, 16T25, 81R50.
  Key words and phrases. Braces, Hopf-Galois extensions.
  The second author is supported by the EPSRC grants EP/V008129/1 and EP/R034826/1.

                                                                                 ISSN 1076-9803/2022

                                             494
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS           495

subgroups of the holomorph and they have been studied in connection to flat
manifolds, quantum integrable systems, etc. Further, skew braces were intro-
duced in [11], as a generalisation of braces, and D. Bachiller followed to discover
that there is a connection between skew braces and Hopf-Galois theory which
was further studied in [21].
   The above evidences the value of classifying braces, which is a direction re-
search has taken in recent years. Braces with cyclic additive groups were classi-
fied in [14, 15] and braces of size 𝑝𝑞 and 𝑝2 𝑞 for primes 𝑝 and 𝑞 were classified
in [1] and [9], respectively. All braces of cardinality 𝑝3 have been described by
D. Bachiller [2] and all skew braces of the same size by K. Nejabati Zenouz [13].
In [22] L. Vendramin suggested that the problem of classification of braces of
order 𝑝𝑛 could be tackled by considering 𝔽-braces, which is the framework of
this paper.
   The general aim of our paper is to develop ring theoretic themes in the main
calculations of characterising the braces as opposed to more group theoretic
themes. Our method of choice is constructing braces using generators and re-
lations. Notice that some other methods of constructing braces, for example by
linking two homomorphisms of abelian and multiplicative groups, were con-
sidered in [2, 13]. When constructing braces it is often difficult to check if the
brace compatibility condition, 𝑎◦(𝑏 + 𝑐) + 𝑎 = 𝑎◦𝑏 + 𝑎◦𝑐, holds, because of
the large amount of choices for 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐. This problem is particularly pertinent
for braces which are not right nilpotent. Indeed, several methods exist for char-
acterising all right nilpotent braces of cardinality 𝑝𝑛 , such as an extension by
the socle [2], and by using the group of flows of pre-Lie algebras [17, 20]. How-
ever, these methods are not available to characterise braces which are not right
nilpotent. On the other hand, it was mentioned on page 22 of [22] that braces
with additive group 𝐶𝑝5 , for 𝑝 = 2, 3, pose a special difficulty for the GAP pack-
age. In this paper we construct all braces of cardinality 𝑝4 which are not right
nilpotent and whose additive group is 𝐶𝑝4 . We hope that similar methods could
be applied in future to help with GAP calculations for braces of cardinality 𝑝5
and 𝑝6 . Problem 2.18 from [22], which asks to compute automorphisms groups
of skew left braces of size 𝑝𝑛 , could also be related for the special case of 𝑛 = 4.
A motivation for aforementioned investigations was mentioned in [2] “for any
brace structure that we can determine, we are also computing a solution to the
Yang-Baxter equation. Another important thing about braces is their connec-
tion with other algebraic structures. For all these reasons, a classification of all
finite braces of finite order is wanted.”
   We also partially answer a question asked in [22], namely the characterisa-
tion of all skew braces of cardinality 𝑝𝑛 (Problem 2.14, [22]). Our main result is
Theorem 6.3, which describes all 𝔽𝑝 -braces of cardinality 𝑝4 which are not right
nilpotent. Our results hold for 𝑝 > 3 and braces of cardinality 𝑝4 for 𝑝 = 2, 3
can be calculated using the GAP package. Notice that finite 𝔽𝑝 -braces are ex-
actly skew braces whose additive group is 𝐶𝑝𝑛 (see the Background Information
496             D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

section below for more details). We also investigate connections of our results
with Hopf-Galois extensions.

2. Background information
   Recall that a set 𝐴 with binary operations + and ∗ is a left brace if (𝐴, +)
is an abelian group and the following version of distributivity combined with
associativity holds:
               (𝑎 + 𝑏 + 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏) ∗ 𝑐 = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑐 + 𝑏 ∗ 𝑐 + 𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ 𝑐),               (1)
                        𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 + 𝑐) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑎 ∗ 𝑐
for all 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴. Moreover, (𝐴, ◦) is a group, where we define
                              𝑎◦𝑏 = 𝑎 + 𝑏 + 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏.
   In what follows, we will use the definition in terms of operation ‘◦’ presented
in [6] (see [16] for the original definition): a set 𝐴 with binary operations of
addition +, and multiplication ◦ is a brace if (𝐴, +) is an abelian group, (𝐴, ◦)
is a group and for every 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴
                           𝑎◦(𝑏 + 𝑐) + 𝑎 = 𝑎◦𝑏 + 𝑎◦𝑐.
Circle algebras related to braces were introduced by Catino and Rizzo in [5].
A special case of circle algebras are radical circle algebras. Notice that radical
circle algebras satisfy the definition 2 from [17], and hence radical circle alge-
bras are exactly right 𝔽-braces. To obtain the corresponding brace, we change
the multiplication to the opposite multiplication in our brace, 𝑎◦𝑏 → 𝑏◦𝑎. We
now recall definition 2 from [17], which we state for left braces, as it was origi-
nally stated for right braces.
Definition 2.1. Let 𝔽 be a field. We say that a left brace 𝐴 is an 𝔽-brace if its
additive group is an 𝔽-vector space such that 𝑎 ∗ (𝛼𝑏) = 𝛼(𝑎 ∗ 𝑏) for all 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴,
𝛼 ∈ 𝔽. Here 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 = 𝑎◦𝑏 − 𝑎 − 𝑏.
   Notice that finite left 𝔽𝑝 -braces are exactly braces whose multiplicative group
is 𝐶𝑝𝑛 , where 𝐶𝑝 is the cyclic group of cardinality 𝑝. Indeed, if 𝐴 is an 𝔽𝑝 -brace
then it is a vector space over 𝔽𝑝 , hence 𝑝𝑎 = 0𝑎 = (𝑝 − 𝑝)𝑎 = 𝑝𝑎 − 𝑝𝑎 = 0𝐴
where 0𝐴 is the identity of the additive group (𝐴, +), and 𝑝𝑎 is the multiplica-
tion of 𝑝 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 and 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴 in our vector space. Note that 1𝑎 = 𝑎 for 1 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 by
the definition of a vector space. Therefore, every element in (𝐴, +) has order
at most 𝑝, and since (𝐴, +) is abelian it follows that (𝐴, +) is 𝐶𝑝𝑛 . On the other
hand, let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace whose additive group is 𝐶𝑝𝑛 , then we can define
1𝑎 = 𝑎 for 1 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 and 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴, and it gives a well defined 𝔽𝑝 -brace. Observe that
the compatibility relation 𝑏 ∗ (𝑖𝑎) = 𝑖(𝑏 ∗ 𝑎) holds in this brace for integers 𝑖,
because 𝑏 ∗ (𝑖𝑎) = 𝑏 ∗ (𝑎 + … + 𝑎) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + … + 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 = 𝑖(𝑎 ∗ 𝑏)
by the brace relation 𝑥 ∗ (𝑦 + 𝑧) = 𝑥 ∗ 𝑦 + 𝑥 ∗ 𝑧. Since 𝑎 ≠ 0 has the additive
order 𝑝, then 𝑝𝑎 = 𝑎 + 𝑎 + … 𝑎 = 0, hence 𝐴 is an 𝔽𝑝 -brace.
   In [16], Rump introduced left nilpotent and right nilpotent braces and radical
chains 𝐴𝑖+1 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 and 𝐴(𝑖+1) = 𝐴(𝑖) ∗ 𝐴 for a left brace 𝐴, where 𝐴 =
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS             497

𝐴1 = 𝐴(1) . Recall that a left brace 𝐴 is left nilpotent if there is a number 𝑛
such that 𝐴𝑛 = 0, where inductively 𝐴𝑖 consists of sums of elements 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 with
𝑎 ∈ 𝐴, 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴𝑖−1 . A left brace 𝐴 is right nilpotent if there is a number 𝑛 such that
𝐴(𝑛) = 0, where 𝐴(𝑖) consists of sums of elements 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 with 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴(𝑖−1) , 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴.
Strongly nilpotent braces and the chain of ideals 𝐴[𝑖] of a brace 𝐴 were defined
                                           ∑𝑖
in [18]. Define 𝐴[1] = 𝐴 and 𝐴[𝑖+1] = 𝑗=1 𝐴[𝑗] ∗ 𝐴[𝑖+1−𝑗] . A left brace 𝐴 is
strongly nilpotent if there is a number 𝑛 such that 𝐴[𝑛] = 0, where 𝐴[𝑖] consists
of sums of elements 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 with 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴[𝑗] , 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴[𝑖−𝑗] for all 0 < 𝑗 < 𝑖.
   All braces and 𝔽𝑝 -braces considered in this paper are left braces.

3. Groups and braces
   In Example 2 in [16], Rump gave an example of a right brace which is right
but not left nilpotent. By taking the opposite multiplication in this brace, we
obtain a left brace of cardinality 24 which is left but not right nilpotent. More-
over, this brace is an 𝔽2 -brace as it is a vector space over 𝔽2 . In this section, we
show that for a prime number 𝑝 > 3, multiplicative groups of left 𝔽𝑝 -braces of
cardinality 𝑝4 which are not right nilpotent are isomorphic to either group XIV
or group XV described below.
   We first recall a result of David Bachiller from [3].
Theorem 3.1 (Lemma 2.5.1, [3]). Let 𝑝 be a prime number, and let (𝐵, +, ◦) be
a finite left brace with (𝐵, +) isomorphic to 𝐶𝑝𝑚 . Assume 𝑚 + 1 ≤ 𝑝. Then, the
order of each non-trivial element in the multiplicative group (𝐵, ◦) is equal 𝑝.
   Therefore, every element in the multiplicative group of any 𝔽𝑝 -brace of car-
dinality 𝑝4 for 𝑝 > 3 has order 𝑝. In [4], Burnside described all groups of
cardinality 𝑝4 for prime 𝑝 > 3.
   Notice that if a brace 𝐴 of cardinality 𝑝4 has an abelian multiplicative group
(𝐴, ◦) then it is a ring, and hence it is both left and right nilpotent [6]. Therefore,
a left nilpotent 𝔽𝑝 -brace which is left but not right nilpotent has a non-abelian
multiplicative group. Therefore, using the list from pages 100, 101 from [4], we
have the following possibilities of non-abelian groups of cardinality 𝑝4 in which
each element has order 𝑝.
       ∙ (Group XIV) Group (with multiplication ◦) generated by elements 𝑃,
         𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 which is the direct product of the group generated by 𝑄 and the
         group generated by elements 𝑃, 𝑅, 𝑆. Moreover, 𝑃◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑆 =
         𝑆◦𝑃, 𝑄◦𝑃 = 𝑃◦𝑄 and 𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑃.
       ∙ (Group XV) Group (with multiplication ◦) generated by elements 𝑃, 𝑄,
         𝑅, 𝑆 with 𝑃 being in the centre of this group, and the centre of this group
         consists of elements 𝑃𝑖 . Moreover, 𝑅◦𝑄 = 𝑄◦𝑅 and 𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃 and
         𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄.
Observe that group XIV has centre of cardinality 𝑝2 and group 𝑋𝑉 has centre
of cardinality 𝑝, where by centre we mean the set of elements which commute
under operation ◦ with all elements in 𝐴.
498              D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

  We shall let 𝑝 be a prime number larger than 3. The aim of this paper is to
characterise all not right nilpotent 𝔽𝑝 -braces of cardinality 𝑝4 . We describe our
method for groups of cardinality 𝑝𝑛 for any 𝑛, as we hope that our approach
could be perhaps applied in some other situations.
     ∙ Let 𝐺 be a group of order 𝑝𝑛 and 𝑔1 , 𝑔2 , … , 𝑔𝑛 be its generators. Let
       𝑓1 , 𝑓2 , … , 𝑓𝑛 be the defining relations of our group 𝐺.
     ∙ We will characterise 𝔽𝑝 -braces 𝐴 for which 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑔1 +𝔽𝑝 𝑔2 +…+𝔽𝑛 𝑔𝑛 .
                               ∑
     ∙ We write 𝑔𝑖 ∗ 𝑔𝑗 = 0<𝑘≤𝑛 𝛼𝑖,𝑗,𝑘 𝑔𝑘 where 𝛼𝑖,𝑗,𝑘 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 are unknown. As
       usual 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 = 𝑎◦𝑏 − 𝑎 − 𝑏 in our brace.
     ∙ We substitute these equations in the relations 𝑓1 , 𝑓2 , … , 𝑓𝑛 as well as
       in the relations 𝑓𝑖 ∗ 𝑔𝑗 for 𝑖, 𝑗 ≤ 𝑛 and find 𝛼𝑖,𝑗,𝑘 such that the above
       equations hold. This gives necessary conditions for our brace to be well-
       defined.
     ∙ To check if the brace is well-defined, we proceed as follows: We consider
       the linear space 𝐵 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑔1′ +… 𝔽𝑝 𝑔𝑛′ for some elements 𝑔1′ , 𝑔2′ , … , 𝑔𝑛′ from
       some set 𝑋. We define maps
                                                ∑
                             𝜆𝑔𝑖 (𝑔𝑗′ ) = 𝑔𝑗′ +   𝛼𝑖,𝑗,𝑘 𝑔𝑘′ .
                                            0<𝑘≤𝑛

      ∙ Next, we define maps 𝜆𝑔 for 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 inductively by using the formula
        𝜆𝑔◦ℎ (𝑏) = 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆ℎ (𝑏)) for 𝑏 ∈ 𝐵. To construct a well defined brace, we
        then use Theorem 2.1 from [8] with the cocycle 𝑓(𝑔) = 𝜆𝑔 (1)−1. Notice
        that, to be able to apply Theorem 2.1, we need to show that 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 → 𝐵
        is a bijective cocycle. In our case it is done in section 5.3.
      ∙ In this way, we can construct all 𝔽𝑝 -braces with multiplicative group 𝐺
        and generators 𝑔1′ , 𝑔2′ , … , 𝑔𝑛′ and such that 𝐺 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑔1′ + … + 𝔽𝑝 𝑔𝑛′ (see
        Section 6 for a method).
      ∙ For braces with multiplicative group XV, we can show that we can as-
        sume that 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑔1 + … + 𝔽𝑝 𝑔𝑛 , provided that the brace is not right
        nilpotent. This then implies that we constructed all not right nilpotent
        braces with the multiplicative group 𝐺.
      ∙ We also show that all 𝔽𝑝 -braces with multiplicative group XIV are right
        nilpotent, and hence strongly nilpotent. Braces of cardinality 𝑝4 for 𝑝 =
        2, 3 can be calculated using the GAP package.

4. Braces whose multiplicative group is XV
  Let (𝐺, ◦) be the group XV, so the free group generated by elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆
subject to relations
                                𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃,
                                    𝑄◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑄,
                      𝑃◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑄 = 𝑄◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑃,
                                   𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄.
                             𝑃𝑝 = 𝑄𝑝 = 𝑅𝑝 = 𝑆 𝑝 = 1𝐺 .
      SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS         499

Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace whose multiplicative group is 𝐺. As usual we have
𝑔◦ℎ = 𝑔 ∗ ℎ + 𝑔 + ℎ.
  We assume that 𝐴 is not right nilpotent. We recall a result of Rump [16].
Theorem 4.1 ([16]). If 𝐴 is a brace of a cardinality 𝑝𝑛 for some prime number
𝑝 and some natural 𝑛, then 𝐴𝑛+1 = 0 where 𝐴1 = 𝐴 and 𝐴𝑖+1 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 .
  We get the following Corollary.
Corollary 4.2. Let 𝐴 be a brace of cardinality 𝑝4 . If 𝐴4 ≠ 0, then 𝐴𝑖 ∕𝐴𝑖+1 has
cardinality 𝑝 for 𝑖 = 1, ..., 4.
Proof. Notice that if 𝐴𝑖 ∕𝐴𝑖+1 has cardinality smaller than 𝑝, then 𝐴𝑖 = 𝐴𝑖+1 ,
since 𝐴𝑖 is an abelian group under the operation +. Suppose that 𝐴𝑖 = 𝐴𝑖+1 for
some 𝑖. Then 𝐴𝑖 = 𝐴𝑖+1 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴𝑖+1 for some 𝑖 < 4. Then 𝐴𝑖 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 =
𝐴 ∗ 𝐴𝑖+1 = 𝐴𝑖+2 . Continuing in this way we get that 𝐴𝑖 = 𝐴4 = 𝐴5 = 0,
which is a contradiction, since we assumed that 𝐴𝑛 ≠ 0. Now we find a chain
of subgroups of index at least 𝑝 given by 𝐴4 ⊂ 𝐴3 ⊂ 𝐴2 ⊂ 𝐴 which implies that
𝐴𝑖 ∕𝐴𝑖+1 has cardinality 𝑝 since the size of 𝐴 is 𝑝4 .                      
Notation 4.3. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace. For an element 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴 we will denote
by 𝑎−1 an element in 𝐴 such that 𝑎◦𝑎−1 = 1 = 0. Similarly, by 𝑎𝑛 , sometimes
written at 𝑎𝑛◦ , we will denote the product of 𝑛 elements 𝑎 under the operation ◦.
  Note that in any brace the identity element 0 of the additive group (𝐴, +)
coincides with the identity element 1 of the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦).

4.1. Some supporting lemmas. Recall that the 𝜆 map in a brace (𝐴, +, ◦) is
defined for 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴 by
                         𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑏 = 𝑎◦𝑏 − 𝑎.
It is known that
                              𝜆𝑎◦𝑏 (𝑐) = 𝜆𝑎 (𝜆𝑏 (𝑐)) .
Lemma 4.4. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 . Then for 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴 we have
       ( −1 −1        )
        𝑎 ◦𝑏 ◦𝑎◦𝑏 ∗ 𝑐 = 𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ 𝑐) − 𝑏 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ 𝑐)
                               + 𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ 𝑐)) + 𝑏 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ 𝑐))
                               − 𝑏 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ 𝑐)) − 𝑎 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ 𝑐)) .
Proof. Note we have 𝐴5 = 0. Now using properties of 𝜆 and the formula
       𝜆𝑎−1 (𝑏) = 𝑏 − 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑎 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ 𝑏) − 𝑎 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ (𝑎 ∗ 𝑏)) for 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝐴
the result follows by computation.                                              
  Recall that in group XV we have the relation
                              𝑄 = 𝑅−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑅◦𝑆.
Now, Lemma 4.4 implies the following.
500               D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

Corollary 4.5. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace whose multiplicative
group is the group XV. Then
                              𝑄 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆ 𝐴𝑖+2 , 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 .
Moreover,
                              𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 ∈ 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴2 ⊆ 𝐴4 .
      Furthermore, using the relation in group XV
                                𝑃 = 𝑄−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑄◦𝑆,
Lemma 4.4, and Corollary 4.5 we have the following corollary.
Corollary 4.6. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace whose multiplicative group is the group
XV. Then
                              𝑃 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆ 𝐴𝑖+3 , 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 .
Therefore,
𝑃 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0, 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 ⊆ 𝐴4 , 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴2 ∗ 𝑃 = 0.
Proposition 4.7. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace which is not right
nilpotent with multiplicative group XV. Then 𝐴4 ≠ 0 and
                                      𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 .
Moreover, 𝐴2 is a brace of cardinality 𝑝3 and 𝐴3 is a brace of cardinality 𝑝2 , so
                                  𝐴3 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 .
Proof. Observe first that 𝑃 ∗ 𝑎 = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑃 for any 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴 since 𝑃 is central in
(𝐴, ◦). Recall 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 , so 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 ⊆ 𝐴4 . Therefore, 𝐴4 = 0 implies
that 𝐼 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 is an ideal in 𝐴 and 𝐼 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐼 = 0. Notice that 𝐴∕𝐼 has
cardinality 𝑝3 , and it is known that this implies that 𝐴∕𝐼 is right nilpotent [3].
Now 𝐴 ∗ 𝐼 = 𝐼 ∗ 𝐴 = 0 implies that 𝐴 is right nilpotent. This contradicts the
assumption that 𝐴 is not right nilpotent.
   We will now show that 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 . If 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 , then 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0, and since 𝑃
is central, we have 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 0. Therefore, reasoning similarly to above, 𝐼 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃
is an ideal in 𝐴 and 𝐴∕𝐼 is right nilpotent. Therefore, 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 .
   Notice that, by Corollary 4.2, 𝐴4 ≠ 0 implies 𝐴𝑖 ∕𝐴𝑖+1 is one dimensional
vector space for 𝑖 = 1, 2, 3, 4. It follows that 𝐴2 is a brace of cardinality 𝑝3 and
𝐴3 has cardinality 𝑝2 , so 𝐴3 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 .                                        
Proposition 4.8. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace which is not right
nilpotent with multiplicative group XV and let 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴4 . Then
                                    𝑎 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑃𝛼 ,
for some 1 ≤ 𝛼 ≤ 𝑝.
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS           501

Proof. Consider the element 𝑒 = 𝑎−1 ◦𝑄−1 ◦𝑎◦𝑄 where the inverses are taken
in the group (𝐴, ◦). Notice that since 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆ 𝐴𝑖+2 and by Lemma 4.4 we get
                              𝑒 ∈ 𝐴3 , 𝑒 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆ 𝐴𝑖+3 .
For 𝑟 ∈ 𝐴 denote
                            𝐸𝑟 = 𝑒−1 ◦𝑟−1 ◦𝑒◦𝑟.
Now using similar reasoning as before we get
                           𝐸𝑟 ∈ 𝐴4 , 𝐸𝑟 ∗ 𝐴 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0.
Since 𝐸𝑟 ∈ 𝐴4 , then 𝐴 ∗ 𝐸𝑟 = 0. This implies that 𝔽𝑝 𝐸𝑟 is an ideal in 𝐴.
Therefore, if 𝐸𝑟 ≠ 0, then 𝐴∕𝔽𝑝 𝐸𝑟 is a brace of cardinality 𝑝3 or less, and hence
it is right nilpotent by [3]. This implies that 𝐴 is right nilpotent. Since we only
consider not right nilpotent braces, this is impossible. Therefore, 𝐸𝑟 = 0. This
holds for every 𝑟 ∈ 𝑅, so it follows that 𝑒 is in the centre of group (𝐴, ◦). Because
the group (𝐴, ◦) is group 𝑋𝑉, it follows that 𝑒 = 𝑃𝑖 for some natural number
𝑖. Therefore, by writing 𝑒 as sums of products of 𝑄 and 𝑎 and using the fact
that 𝐴 ∗ 𝑎 = 0 since 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴4 we get 𝑎 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑃𝛼 , for some 0 ≤ 𝛼 < 𝑝 (since
𝐴3 ∗ 𝐴3 = 𝐴3 ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 ) = 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴3 = 0).                                         
Proposition 4.9. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace which is not
right nilpotent with multiplicative group XV. Suppose that 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 and 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴3 .
Then there exist element 𝑆̄ ∈ 𝐴4 such that the mapping 𝑓 ∶ (𝐴, ◦) → (𝐴, ◦) given
by 𝑓(𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝑓(𝑄) = 𝑄, 𝑓(𝑅) = 𝑅, 𝑓(𝑆) = 𝑆̄ is an automorphism of the group
(𝐴, ◦).
Proof. Observe that the mapping 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐺 of the group 𝐺 = (𝐴, ◦) defined
on generators of 𝐺 by
             𝑓(𝑅) = 𝑅, 𝑓(𝑄) = 𝑄, 𝑓(𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝑓(𝑆) = 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑘
is a group homomorphism for any 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘.
   Observe that since 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 , then for some 𝑖 the element 𝑆2 ∶= 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 will
belong to 𝐴2 (because by Corollary 4.6 we have that 𝐴∕𝐴2 has dimension 1 as
an 𝔽𝑝 -vector space). Notice also that since 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴3 , then for some 𝑗 element
𝑆3 ∶= 𝑆2 ◦𝑄𝑗 will belong to 𝐴3 .
   We know that 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 and 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 . Consequently, for some 𝑘 we have that
element 𝑆4 = 𝑆3 ◦𝑃𝑘 will be in 𝐴4 . Therefore, 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑘 ∈ 𝐴4 . We can now
define 𝑆̄ = 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑘 .
   It remains to show that 𝑓 is an automorphism, so the kernel of 𝑓 is trivial.
This follows because the image of a non-trivial element 𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑅𝛾 ◦𝑆 𝜉 will be
a non-trivial element (alternatively, it is easy to give the formula for the inverse
map 𝑓 −1 ).                                                                       
4.2. The case when 𝑹 ∈ 𝑨𝟐 .
Lemma 4.10. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace whose multi-
plicative group is the group XV. If 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝐴2 is a commutative brace.
502             D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

Proof. Suppose that 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 so 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅 ⊆ 𝐴2 . Since the set {𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑅𝑡 ∶
0 < 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑡 ≤ 𝑝} has cardinality 𝑝3 and is contained in 𝐴2 it follows that 𝐴2 =
{𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑅𝑡 ∶ 0 < 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑡 ≤ 𝑝}, by Proposition 4.7. Therefore, (𝐴2 , ◦) is com-
mutative (since 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅 commute with each other). It follows that (𝐴, +, ∗) is a
commutative ring by [6].                                                      
Lemma 4.11. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace which is not right nilpotent with multi-
plicative group XV. If 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = 0.
Proof. Notice that from the relation
                                 𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄
we get
                      𝑅 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑄.
therefore,
         𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄) + 𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑄) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄
         𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴4 since 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 .                (2)
We have also the group relation 𝑄◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑄, therefore
                            (𝑄◦𝑅) ∗ 𝑆 = (𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑆,
which implies that 𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆). Now
                           𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴 3 = 𝔽𝑃 𝑃 + 𝐴 4 ,
so 𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) ∈ 𝔽𝑃 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 0. Thus substituting in (2) we find
             0 = 𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄,
since we have assumed 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 , we have that 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) = 0, so 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = 0. 
Proposition 4.12. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace which is not right nilpotent with
multiplicative group XV. If 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴3 .
Proof. Suppose on the contrary that 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴3 . Recall that, by Corollaries 4.5
and 4.6 and Proposition 4.7, 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 , 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 , 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 . Hence,
                            𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 .
In group XV we have the relation
                                𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃,
hence 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃, by Corollary 4.6. We also have the relation
𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄, so
                      𝑅 ∗𝑆 =𝑆 ∗𝑅+𝑆 ∗𝑄+𝑅 ∗𝑄+𝑄
(notice that 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑄) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) ∈ 𝑆 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0). Also, we have the
relation
                           (𝑅◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑆 = (𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑆,
hence,
                𝑅 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆.
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS          503

  Observe that 𝑅 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) ⊆ 𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 . Recall that 𝐴2 is a commutative ring by
Lemma 4.10 and 𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 , hence
  𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴2 ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 ) ⊆ 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝐴2 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴4 = 0
(since 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = 0 by Lemma 4.11 and 𝐴2 is commutative). Next, by the above
we have
              𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑄).
Therefore,
      𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = −(𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄) + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆)) ⊆ 𝐴4 .
Recall from the beginning of this proof that 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 − 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃, so
                                         −𝑃
                                 𝑆∗𝑄∈       + 𝐴4 .
                                          2
                     𝑃
Therefore, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 ∈ + 𝐴4 .
                    2
  Recall the relation
                      (𝑄◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑆 = (𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑆.
Hence, 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆, and by the above
                      𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) ⊆ 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴2 ⊆ 𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0,
                             𝑃             𝑆∗𝑃               3
and 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) ∈ 𝑆 ∗ ( + 𝐴4 ) =              . Therefore, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0. Hence
                              2             2             2
𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 so 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 is an ideal in 𝐴. Consequently, 𝐴∕𝔽𝑝 𝑃 is right
nilpotent, so 𝐴 is right nilpotent, a contradiction.                     

4.3. The case when 𝑸 ∈ 𝑨𝟑 .
Theorem 4.13. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace whose mul-
tiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XV. Suppose that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴3 . Then 𝐴 is a right
nilpotent brace.
Proof. Notice that the set of all products 𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 has cardinality 𝑝2 , and we know
from Proposition 4.7 that 𝐴3 = 𝐴 ∗ (𝐴 ∗ 𝐴) has cardinality 𝑝2 . Moreover,
𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ∈ 𝐴3 (where 𝑃𝑗 = 𝑃◦ ⋯ ◦𝑃, where 𝑃 appears 𝑗 times in this product).
So 𝐴3 = {𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ∶ 𝑖, 𝑗 ≤ 𝑝}. Since 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴3 , it follows that there are integers 𝑖, 𝑗
and 0 ≠ 𝐸 ∈ 𝐴4 such that
                                    𝐸 = 𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 .
  We will now consider two cases.
  Case 1. Either 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴2 or both 𝑆, 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 . Because 𝐴∕𝐴2 has dimension 1.
Then there is 0 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑝 such that
                                   𝑆◦𝑅𝑗 ∈ 𝐴2 .
Denote 𝑍 = 𝑆◦𝑅𝑗 .
  By the group relations, we have
                                 𝑄◦𝑍 = 𝑍◦𝑄◦𝑃.
504              D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

Recall that 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, so

                            𝑄 ∗ 𝑍 = 𝑍 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑍 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃.

Notice 𝑄 ∗ 𝑍 ∈ 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴2 ⊆ 𝐴4 and 𝑍 ∗ 𝑄 ⊆ 𝑍 ∗ 𝐴3 ⊆ 𝐴4 , 𝑍 ∗ 𝑃 ⊆ 𝑍 ∗ 𝐴3 ⊆ 𝐴4 ,
so
                                     𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 .
But 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 implies that 𝐴 is nilpotent, as shown previously.
  Case 2. Suppose 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴, 𝑆 ∉ 𝐴2 and 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 .
  Observe that the group relation

                                  𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃

implies
                            𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃,
since 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 by Corollary 4.6. Therefore,

             𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄) + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑃) + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃

since
                      𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄) ⊆ 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝐴3 ) ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0.
Observe now that we also have a relation

                            (𝑄◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑆 = (𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑆,

which implies 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆. By the above, 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗
𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 2𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 (since 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃). Notice that if
𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 then 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 and similarly as in previous section it
implies that 𝐴 is right nilpotent. If 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 ≠ 0, then 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) ≠ 0. Notice that
𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 . Therefore,

        𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) ⊆ 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅,

since 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴3 . It follows that 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 ≠ 0.
   Note that because 𝑅◦𝑄 = 𝑄◦𝑅 we get 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 ≠ 0. Observe that by
the above there are 𝑖, 𝑗 such that 𝑄𝑖 ◦𝑃𝑗 = 𝐸 ∈ 𝐴4 , where 𝑖 is a natural number
not divisible by 𝑝, since 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 , as 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 would imply that 𝐴 is a right
nilpotent brace (for example by the first Lemma in Section 8). Observe that it
follows that 𝐸 ∗ 𝑅 = (𝑄𝑖 ◦𝑃𝑗 ) ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑖(𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) ≠ 0 (since 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 ⊆ 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0).
On the other hand, since 𝑅, 𝑃, 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 and 𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝3 then 𝐴2 is
commutative. Therefore, 𝐸 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴2 ∗ 𝐸 ⊆ 𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0, which is a
contradiction. Notice that 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 so 𝐸 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0 gives 𝐸 ∗ 𝑅 = 0. However, we
have shown that 𝐸 ∗ 𝑅 is not zero above. This gives a contradiction.          
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS                    505

4.4. The case when 𝑺 ∈ 𝑨𝟒 .
Proposition 4.14. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace whose
multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XV. Then (𝐴, ◦) is generated by elements
𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 which satisfy relations from group XV. Moreover, the following relations
hold for 𝑎 ∈ {𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆}.
    (1)
                   𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃, (𝑄◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑎
    (2)
                       𝑄◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑄, (𝑄◦𝑅) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑎
    (3)
                      𝑃◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑄 = 𝑄◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑃,
(𝑃◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑆◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑎 = 0, (𝑃◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑄◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑎 = 0, (𝑃◦𝑅) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑅◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑎
    (4)
                    𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄, (𝑅◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑎
    (5)
   𝑃𝑝 = 𝑄𝑝 = 𝑅𝑝 = 𝑆 𝑝 = 0, (𝑃𝑝 ) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑄𝑝 ) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑅𝑝 ) ∗ 𝑎 = (𝑆 𝑝 ) ∗ 𝑎 = 0
Proof. It follows from the fact that group XV is the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦)
of our brace. Recall that 0 is the identity element of the additive group (𝐴, +)
and also the identity element of the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) (these identity
elements coincide in every brace).                                            
Proposition 4.15. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace
which is not right nilpotent with multiplicative group XV. Then (𝐴, ◦) is generated
by elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 which satisfy relations from group XV. In addition, we have
the following.
    (1) 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴4 , 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 , 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 , 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 . Moreover, 𝑄 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆ 𝐴𝑖+2 , 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴𝑖 ⊆
         𝐴𝑖+3 .
    (2) 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴3 , 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴, 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 .
    (3) 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑦𝑆 for some 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with
         𝑦 ≠ 0.
    (4) 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 0, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑆 = 0, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑆 = 0.
    (5) 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝛼𝑆, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝛾𝑃, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑧1 𝑃 + 𝑧𝑆 for some
         𝛼, 𝛾, 𝑧, 𝑧1 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 .
    (6) 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑧1 𝑃 + 𝑧𝑆, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑦𝑆 for some 𝑧, 𝑧1 , 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0.
    (7) 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑗 ′ 𝑄 + 𝑖 ′ 𝑃 + 𝑘 ′ 𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑗𝑄 + 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆 for some 𝑗, 𝑗 ′ , 𝑖, 𝑖 ′ , 𝑘, 𝑘 ′ ∈
         𝔽𝑝 .
    (8) 𝛾 = −1.
    (9) 𝛼 = −𝑦.
   (10) 𝑗 ′ = −1.
   (11) 𝑧1 = 0 and 𝑗 = 0.
   (12) 2𝑧 = 𝑦, 𝑖 ′ = 1, 𝑘 ′ = −𝑧.
Proof.        (1) It follows from Corollary 4.5, Proposition 4.7, Proposition 4.9.
506                D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

       (2) It follows from Proposition 4.12 and Theorem 4.13.
       (3) It follows from Corollary 4.5 that 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑃, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴5 = 0 (since
           𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 as 𝑆◦𝑃 = 𝑃◦𝑆). Moreover, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑆, which
           gives the conclusion.
       (4) It follows from the fact that 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴4 so 𝐴 ∗ 𝑆 = 0.
       (5) By Corollary 4.5, we have that 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴5 = 0, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴4 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑆.
           Similarly, since 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴3 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆, by item 1
           above. The fact that 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝛾𝑃 follows from Proposition 4.8.
       (6) Since 𝑃 is central in the group XV it follows that 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑦𝑆
           by item 3 above. Similarly, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 since 𝑄◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑄, and the
           result follows from item 5 above.
       (7) Notice that 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 by item 1.
       (8) Consider the relation
                                   𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃 = 𝑄◦𝑆.
           It can be rewritten as 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑃 + 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 0 since 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 ⊆ 𝐴 ∗
           𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0. This gives 𝛾 = −1.
       (9) Consider the relation
                             (𝑅◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑄 = (𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑄.
           We get 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑄) = 𝑅 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄), hence 𝛼 = −𝑦.
      (10) Consider the relation (𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑅 = (𝑄◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑅 which is an implica-
           tion of one of the group relations in group XV. We can rewrite it as
                          𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑄 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅).
           This implies −𝑦 = −𝛼𝑗 ′ . We know that 𝑦 ≠ 0 since 𝐴 is not right
           nilpotent, and 𝛼 = −𝑦, hence 𝑗 ′ = −1.
      (11) We will first show that 𝑗 = −𝑧1 . Consider the group relation 𝑄◦𝑅 =
           𝑅◦𝑄, it implies (𝑄◦𝑅) ∗ 𝑅 = (𝑅◦𝑄) ∗ 𝑅. This implies 𝑄 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑅) =
           𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅), hence 𝑗𝛼 = 𝑧1 𝑦. Since 𝑦 ≠ 0 and 𝑦 = −𝛼 we get 𝑧1 = −𝑗.
               We will now to show that 𝑧1 = 0. Consider the relation (𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄) ∗
           𝑅 = (𝑅◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑅. This implies 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) = 𝑅 ∗
           (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅) since 𝑆 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0. We can consider the component
           corresponding to 𝑃 in this equation. This implies −𝑗 + 𝑧1 = 𝑗 ′ 𝑧1 , and
           since 𝑗 ′ = −1 we get 𝑗 = 2𝑧1 . Since we previously showed that 𝑧1 = −𝑗
           it follows that 𝑧1 = 𝑗 = 0.
      (12) Consider the equation 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑅 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅) = 𝑅 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑅)
           from the previous sub-point. Comparing the component at 𝑆 in this
           equation we get 𝑧 = 𝑧𝑗 ′ + 𝑖 ′ 𝑦, hence 2𝑧 = 𝑖 ′ 𝑦.
               We will now show that 𝑖 ′ = 1 hence 2𝑧 = 𝑦. We will now consider
           the relation
                                    𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄 = 𝑅◦𝑆.
           This implies
                           𝑆 ∗𝑅+𝑆 ∗𝑄+𝑅 ∗𝑄+𝑄=0
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS                507

        since 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑄) ⊆ 𝑆 ∗ 𝐴3 = 0 and 𝑅 ∗ 𝑆 ⊆ 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴4 = 𝐴5 = 0.
        Comparing the component at 𝑃 in this equation we get 𝑖 ′ −1 = 0, hence
        𝑖 ′ = 1, as required. Comparing component at 𝑆 we get 𝑘 ′ + 𝑧 = 0 hence
        𝑘′ = −𝑧.

Remark 4.16. A general comment on Proposition 4.15 to explain the approach.
In first subpoint we show that
                            𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄
and then so we can write each product, for example 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 as 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑗𝑅 + 𝑘𝑆 + 𝑙𝑄
for some 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘, 𝑙 in 𝔽𝑝 . Next we substitute it to the equations, which need to hold
in the brace, listed in Theorem 4.13, and then list the consequences.

5. The braces are well-defined
5.1. The map 𝝀. We now consider how our operation ∗ looks in our brace.
In the previous section we showed that if (𝐴, +, ◦) is brace which is not right
nilpotent whose group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XV, then
                  𝑃 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
              𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = −𝑦𝑆, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 = 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
           𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 = 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
        𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = −𝑃, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 = −𝑄 + 𝑃 − 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑆 = 0.
where 𝑦, 𝑖, 𝑘 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0.
  Therefore, we get the formulas for the 𝜆 maps in 𝐴, where 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑏.
               𝜆𝑃 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑄) = 𝑄, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
         𝜆𝑄 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑄) = 𝑄 − 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
    𝜆𝑅 (𝑃) = 𝑃 + 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑄) = 𝑄 + 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
     𝜆𝑆 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑄) = 𝑄 − 𝑃, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑅) = 𝑅 − 𝑄 + 𝑃 − 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑆) = 𝑆.
  Let (𝐵′ , +) be the abelian group generated by elements 𝑄′ , 𝑃′ , 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ , 1 where
every element has order 𝑝, so 𝑝𝑄′ = 𝑝𝑄′ = 𝑝𝑅′ = 𝑝𝑆 ′ = 𝑝1 = 0. Therefore,
                      𝐵′ = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃′ + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄′ + 𝔽𝑝 𝑅′ + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 ′ + 𝔽𝑝 1,
where 1 is some element of 𝐵.
   Let (𝐵, +) be the subgroup of (𝐵′ , +) generated by elements 𝑃′ , 𝑄′ , 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ . De-
fine the homomorphisms 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 from (𝐵′ , +) to (𝐵′ , +) by using the table
for 𝜆 maps in 𝐵 above, and by setting 𝜆𝑔 (1) = 𝑔′ + 1 for 𝑔 ∈ {𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆}.
   So we have the following relations which depend on parameters 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝
with 𝑦 ≠ 0 given below.
            𝜆𝑃 (𝑃′ ) = 𝑃′ , 𝜆𝑃 (𝑄′ ) = 𝑄′ , 𝜆𝑃 (𝑅′ ) = 𝑅′ + 𝑦𝑆 ′ , 𝜆𝑃 (𝑆 ′ ) = 𝑆 ′ ,
                                    𝜆𝑃 (1) = 𝑃′ + 1,

        𝜆𝑄 (𝑃′ ) = 𝑃′ , 𝜆𝑄 (𝑄′ ) = 𝑄′ − 𝑦𝑆 ′ , 𝜆𝑄 (𝑅′ ) = 2−1 𝑦𝑆 ′ + 𝑅′ , 𝜆𝑄 (𝑆 ′ ) = 𝑆 ′ ,
                                         𝜆𝑄 (1) = 𝑄′ + 1,

                                   𝜆𝑆 (𝑆 ′ ) = 𝑆 ′ , 𝜆𝑆 (1) = 𝑆 ′ + 1.
Theorem 5.1. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number and 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0.
Let (𝐵′ , +) and (𝐵, +) be defined as above. Then both (𝐵′ , +) and (𝐵, +) are
linear spaces over the field 𝔽𝑝 . Let linear maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵′ , +) ⟶ (𝐵′ , +) for
𝑔 ∈ {𝑅, 𝑄, 𝑃, 𝑆} be defined by lines 1-4 above. Then the following relations hold
for any 𝑎 ∈ 𝐵′ .
    (1)
                           𝜆𝑄 (𝜆𝑆 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑆 (𝜆𝑄 (𝜆𝑃 (𝑎))),
      (2)
                                     𝜆𝑄 (𝜆𝑅 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑅 (𝜆𝑄 (𝑎)),
      (3)
      𝜆𝑃 (𝜆𝑆 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑆 (𝜆𝑃 (𝑎)), 𝜆𝑃 (𝜆𝑄 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑄 (𝜆𝑃 (𝑎)), 𝜆𝑃 (𝜆𝑅 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑅 (𝜆𝑃 (𝑎)),
      (4)
                                  𝜆𝑅 (𝜆𝑆 (𝑎)) = 𝜆𝑆 (𝜆𝑅 (𝜆𝑄 (𝑎))),
      (5)
                              𝑝          𝑝          𝑝          𝑝
                            𝜆𝑃 (𝑎) = 𝜆𝑄 (𝑎) = 𝜆𝑅 (𝑎) = 𝜆𝑆 (𝑎) = 𝑎.
Therefore, the maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵′ , +) ⟶ (𝐵′ , +) defined inductively using the for-
mula
                            𝜆𝑔◦𝑔′ (𝑎) = 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆𝑔′ (𝑎))
for 𝑔, 𝑔′ ∈ (𝐺, ◦) and 𝑎 ∈ (𝐵′ , +) are well defined automorphisms of 𝐵′ . More-
over, maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ 𝐵 ⟶ 𝐵 with the domain restricted to 𝐵 are automorphisms of
(𝐵, +).
Proof. To check these properties we will present the 𝜆 maps in matrix form,
and the above properties can be checked by multiplying the matrices 𝑀𝑔 . Write
the matrices of the linear maps 𝜆𝑔 for 𝑔 ∈ {𝑅, 𝑄, 𝑃, 𝑆} in the base 𝑒1 = 1, 𝑒2 =
𝑅′ , 𝑒3 = 𝑄′ , 𝑒4 = 𝑃′ , 𝑒5 = 𝑆 ′ where 𝑒𝑖 denotes the vector with all entries zero
except of the 𝑖-th entry which is 1. Therefore, we have matrices 𝑀𝑖 of dimension
5 such that 𝜆𝑔 (𝑒𝑗 ) = 𝑀𝑔 𝑒𝑗 for each 𝑔 ∈ {𝑅, 𝑄, 𝑃, 𝑆} where 𝑒1 = 1, 𝑒2 = 𝑅′ , 𝑒3 =
𝑄′ , 𝑒4 = 𝑃′ , 𝑒5 = 𝑆 ′ .

  We have the matrices

observe now that, by direct calculation, we have
                       𝑀𝑄 𝑀𝑆 = 𝑀𝑆 𝑀𝑄 𝑀𝑃 , 𝑀𝑄 𝑀𝑅 = 𝑀𝑅 𝑀𝑄 ,

              𝑀𝑃 𝑀𝑆 = 𝑀𝑆 𝑀𝑃 , 𝑀𝑃 𝑀𝑄 = 𝑀𝑄 𝑀𝑃 , 𝑀𝑃 𝑀𝑅 = 𝑀𝑅 𝑀𝑃 ,

                                    𝑀𝑅 𝑀𝑆 = 𝑀𝑆 𝑀𝑅 𝑀𝑄 ,
                                𝑝        𝑝       𝑝       𝑝
                            𝑀𝑃 = 𝑀𝑄 = 𝑀𝑅 = 𝑀𝑆 = 𝐼𝑑,
where 𝐼𝑑 is the identity matrix. This proves the first part of our theorem.
   We can now define maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵′ , +) ⟶ (𝐵′ , +) inductively, using the
formula
                                    𝜆𝑔◦𝑔′ (𝑎) = 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆𝑔′ (𝑎)),
for 𝑔, 𝑔′ ∈ (𝐺, ◦) and 𝑎 ∈ (𝐵′ , +). Observe that the maps 𝜆𝑔 are group ho-
momorphisms of (𝐵′ , +) so they are linear maps over the field 𝔽𝑝 , so 𝜆𝑔 (𝑎 +
𝑏) = 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) + 𝜆𝑔 (𝑏). This is because they are defined as compositions of maps
𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 which are homomorphisms of (𝐵′ , +), so
            𝜆𝑃 (𝑎 + 𝑏) = 𝜆𝑃 (𝑎) + 𝜆𝑃 (𝑏), 𝜆𝑄 (𝑎 + 𝑏) = 𝜆𝑄 (𝑎) + 𝜆𝑄 (𝑏),
            𝜆𝑅 (𝑎 + 𝑏) = 𝜆𝑅 (𝑎) + 𝜆𝑅 (𝑏), 𝜆𝑆 (𝑎 + 𝑏) = 𝜆𝑆 (𝑎) + 𝜆𝑆 (𝑏).
  Notice that maps 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 are linear maps and can be represented by
matrices, therefore their compositions are also linear maps. Consequently, for
any 𝑔, ℎ, 𝑗 ∈ 𝐺
               𝜆(𝑔◦ℎ)◦𝑗 = 𝜆𝑔◦ℎ 𝜆𝑗 = (𝜆𝑔 𝜆ℎ )𝜆𝑗 = 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆ℎ 𝜆𝑗 ) = 𝜆𝑔◦(ℎ◦𝑗) .
   We will now show that maps 𝜆𝑔 are automorphisms of 𝐵′ . Notice that the
images of maps 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 are subsets of (𝐵′ , +), and that the kernels of these
maps are zero. Therefore, the maps 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 with the domain restricted to
(𝐵, +) as maps from (𝐵, +) to (𝐵, +) are automorphisms of (𝐵, +). It follows that
maps 𝜆𝑔 with the domain restricted to (𝐵, +) for 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 are also automorphisms
of (𝐵, +) because they are compositions of maps 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 .                  
510               D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

5.2. The map f. Let 𝐵, 𝐵′ and maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵′ , +) ⟶ (𝐵′ , +) be defined as in
Theorem 5.1 for some 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0 and 𝑝 > 3. We will consider
(𝐵, +) as a set 𝐵. Define the map 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐵 by

                                 𝑓(𝑔) = 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1,

for 𝑔 ∈ (𝐺, ◦).

Theorem 5.2. Let 𝐵, 𝐵′ and maps 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵′ , +) ⟶ (𝐵′ , +) be defined as in
Theorem 5.1 for some 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0 and 𝑝 > 3. Then the map 𝑓 ∶
𝐺 ⟶ 𝐵 defined as
                                 𝑓(𝑔) = 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1
for 𝑔 ∈ (𝐺, ◦) is a bijective function from 𝐺 to 𝐵.

Proof. We will now show that 𝑓 is a bijective function. Observe that groups 𝐺
and (𝐵, +) have the same cardinality, so to show that 𝑓 is a bijective function it
suffices to show that 𝑓 is injective.
   Suppose on the contrary that 𝑓 is not bijective. Then we would have 𝑓(𝑔) =
𝑓(ℎ) for some 𝑔, ℎ ∈ 𝐺. This implies 𝜆𝑔 (1) = 𝜆ℎ (1). Let 𝑔′ = ℎ−1 ◦𝑔 so 𝜆𝑔′ (1) =
1. Every element of 𝐺 can be written as a product of elements of some powers of
elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆. Therefore, there are some integers 0 ≤ 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾, 𝜉 < 𝑝 such
that
                                𝑔′ = 𝑅𝛾 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆 𝜉 .
  Notice that it follows from Theorem 5.1 (using the fact that 𝜆𝑎◦𝑏 (𝑐) = 𝜆𝑎 𝜆𝑏 (𝑐)
several times) that 𝜆𝑅𝛾 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆𝜉 (1)−1 = 𝛾𝑅′ +𝐶 where 𝐶 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 𝑄′ +𝔽𝑝 𝑃′ +𝔽𝑝 𝑆 ′ ,
hence
                               𝜆𝑔′ (1) − 1 = 𝛾𝑅′ + 𝐶.
Notice that 𝜆𝑔′ (1) = 1 implies 𝛾 = 0, so

                                  𝑔′ = 𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆 𝜉 .

  Notice that it follows from Theorem 5.1 (using the fact that 𝜆𝑎◦𝑏 (𝑐) = 𝜆𝑎 𝜆𝑏 (𝑐)
several times) that 𝜆𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆𝜉 (1) − 1 = 𝛽𝑄′ + 𝐷 where 𝐷 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 𝑃′ + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 ′ , hence

                               𝜆𝑔′ (1) − 1 = 𝛽𝑄′ + 𝐷.

Notice that 𝜆𝑔′ (1) = 1 implies 𝛽 = 0, so

                                    𝑔′ = 𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆 𝜉 .

   Observe now that by Theorem 5.1 we get 𝜆𝑔′ (1) = 𝜆𝑃𝛼 ◦𝑆𝜉 (1) = 𝛼𝑃′ + 𝜉𝑆 ′ + 1.
Therefore, 𝜆𝑔′ (1) = 1 implies 𝜆 = 𝜉 = 0, so 𝑔′ = 𝑔◦ℎ−1 is the identity element
in 𝐺 ′ , and so 𝑔 = ℎ as required.                                             
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS           511

5.3. Bijective cocycles and braces.
Definition 5.3. Let (𝐺, ◦) be a group, (𝐻, +) be an abelian group, 𝑝 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶
Aut(𝐻) be an action and 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐻 be such that for 𝑔, ℎ ∈ 𝐺 we have
                             𝑓(𝑔◦ℎ) = 𝑓(𝑔) + 𝑝𝑔 (𝑓(ℎ)).
Then 𝑓 is a 1-cocycle with respect to 𝑝𝑔 .
   The following result is known (cf. Jespers, Cedó, Okninski, Rio [8, Theorem
2]).
Theorem 5.4 (Theorem 2, [8]). Let (𝐺, ◦) be a group, (𝐻, +) be an abelian group,
𝑝𝑔 be an automorphism of 𝐻 for each 𝑔 in 𝐺, and 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐻 be a bijective 1-
cocycle with respect to 𝑝. Define an operation on 𝐺 for 𝑔, ℎ ∈ 𝐺 by
                             𝑔 + ℎ = 𝑓 −1 (𝑓(𝑔) + 𝑓(ℎ)) .
Then (𝐺, ◦, +) is a brace.
Theorem 5.5. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let (𝐺, ◦) be the group XV, and
let automorphisms of (𝐵, +), given by 𝜆𝑔 ∶ (𝐵, +) ⟶ (𝐵, +), be defined as in
Theorem 5.1 for fixed 𝑦, 𝑖, 𝑘. Then the group (𝐺, ◦) with the addition defined as
                             𝑔 + ℎ = 𝑓 −1 (𝑓(𝑔) + 𝑓(ℎ)) ,
where 𝑓 is defined as in Theorem 5.2, is a brace.
Proof. By Theorem 5.4, it suffices to show that the map 𝑓 is a bijective cocycle
with respect to the map
                                    𝑝𝑔 = 𝜆𝑔 .
By Theorem 5.2, 𝑓 is a bijective function. To show that 𝑓 is a cocycle, we need
to show that
                           𝑓(𝑔◦ℎ) = 𝑓(𝑔) + 𝑝𝑔 (𝑓(ℎ)).
By using the formula
                               𝑓(𝑔) = 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1,
the left hand side becomes 𝑓(𝑔◦ℎ) = 𝜆𝑔◦ℎ (1) − 1 and the right hand side be-
comes
                             (         )
          𝑓(𝑔) + 𝑝𝑔 (𝑓(ℎ)) = 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1 + 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆ℎ (1) − 1) = 𝜆𝑔◦ℎ (1) − 1
since 𝜆𝑎◦𝑏 (1) = 𝜆𝑎 (𝜆𝑏 (1)) by the definition of 𝜆, and 𝜆𝑔 (𝑥 + 𝑦) = 𝜆𝑔 (𝑥) + 𝜆𝑔 (𝑦)
since 𝜆 is a automorphism of (𝐵′ , +) by Theorem 5.1.                              

6. All braces
   In this section, we show that in Theorem 5.5 we constructed all the 𝔽𝑝 -braces
which are not right nilpotent with multiplicative group XV.
   We will refer to the Multiplicative Table. The following set of rules will be
called the Multiplicative Table.
                 𝑃 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
512               D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

              𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 = −𝑦𝑆, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅 = 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
            𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑄 = 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆, 𝑅 ∗ 𝑆 = 0,
          𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = −𝑃, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 = −𝑄 + 𝑃 − 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑆 = 0.
   Notice, that using the formulas 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑏 we can write the Multi-
plicative Table in the following form.
                𝜆𝑃 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑄) = 𝑄, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑃 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
          𝜆𝑄 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑄) = 𝑄 − 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑄 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
      𝜆𝑅 (𝑃) = 𝑃 + 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑄) = 𝑄 + 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑅) = 𝑅 + 𝑖𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆, 𝜆𝑅 (𝑆) = 𝑆,
       𝜆𝑆 (𝑃) = 𝑃, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑄) = 𝑄 − 𝑃, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑅) = 𝑅 − 𝑄 + 𝑃 − 2−1 𝑦𝑆, 𝜆𝑆 (𝑆) = 𝑆.
We can obtain the Multiplicative Table by putting 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 = 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) − 𝑏.
Theorem 6.1. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be the brace con-
structed in Theorem 5.5 for fixed 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0. Then (𝐴, +, ◦) satisfies
the Multiplicative Table above for the same 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦.
Proof. Let 𝑓(𝑔) = 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1 be defined as in Theorem 5.5. Recall that maps
𝜆𝑔 ∶ 𝐵′ → 𝐵′ were defined in Theorem 5.1. By Theorem 5.1 functions 𝜆𝑔
satisfy relations from above Theorem 5.1. Each of them is of the form 𝜆𝑔 (ℎ′ ) =
𝛼1 𝑅′ + 𝛼2 𝑄′ + 𝛼3 𝑃′ + 𝛼4 𝑆 ′ , for some 𝑔 ∈ {𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆}, ℎ′ ∈ {𝑃′ , 𝑄′ , 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ } and
𝛼1 , 𝛼2 , 𝛼3 , 𝛼4 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 . Let ℎ ∈ 𝐺 be such that 𝜆ℎ (1) − 1 = ℎ′ . Notice, that our
relation can be written as
        (𝜆𝑔◦ℎ (1) − 1) − (𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1) = 𝜆𝑔 (𝜆ℎ (1) − 1)
         = 𝛼1 (𝜆𝑅 (1) − 1) + 𝛼2 (𝜆𝑄 (1) − 1) + 𝛼3 (𝜆𝑃 (1) − 1) + 𝛼4 (𝜆𝑆 (1) − 1).
Since 𝜆𝑔 (1) − 1 = 𝑓(𝑔), we can write it as
              𝑓(𝑔◦ℎ) − 𝑓(𝑔) = 𝛼1 𝑓(𝑅) + 𝛼2 𝑓(𝑄) + 𝛼3 𝑓(𝑃) + 𝛼4 𝑓(𝑆).
So we know that function 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐵 used in Theorem 5.5 satisfies the above
relation. Because 𝑓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ 𝐵 is a bijective function, we can apply the map 𝑓
to both sides of this relation to obtain an equivalent relation
        𝑓 −1 (𝑓(𝑔◦ℎ) − 𝑓(𝑔)) = 𝑓 −1 (𝛼1 𝑓(𝑅) + 𝛼2 𝑓(𝑄) + 𝛼3 𝑓(𝑃) + 𝛼4 𝑓(𝑆)) .
Using the formula for addition in brace (𝐴, +, ◦) from Theorem 5.5, we find
that the relation
                    𝑔◦ℎ − 𝑔 = 𝛼1 𝑅 + 𝛼2 𝑄 + 𝛼3 𝑃 + 𝛼4 𝑆
holds in brace 𝐴. In this way, we can obtain all relations from the Multiplicative
Table.                                                                          
Theorem 6.2. Let 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 be elements of some set 𝒮. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -
brace such that 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 as a linear 𝔽𝑝 -space. Suppose
that elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 satisfy the relations from the Multiplicative Table for fixed
𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0 and 𝑝 > 3. Then the following holds.
      SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS             513

   (1) 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 satisfy the defining relations of the group XV. So the following
       holds.
    𝑄◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑄◦𝑃, 𝑄◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑄, 𝑃◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑄 = 𝑄◦𝑃, 𝑃◦𝑅 = 𝑅◦𝑃,
                   𝑅◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅◦𝑄, 𝑃𝑝 = 𝑄𝑝 = 𝑅𝑝 = 𝑆 𝑝 = 0.
   (2) Every element from 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 can be written in an unique
       way as 𝑅𝛼 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛾 ◦𝑆 𝜉 for some 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾, 𝜉 ≤ 𝑝.
   (3) The multiplication of any two elements from 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 is
       uniquely determined. Therefore, 𝐴 is uniquely determined by the Multi-
       plicative Table and by elements 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦.
   (4) The group (𝐴, ◦) is generated as a group by elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 and it sat-
       isfies the relations of group XV, and it has 𝑝4 elements, hence it is group
       XV.
   (5) The brace (𝐴, +, ◦) is not right nilpotent.
Proof.      (1) It follows from Theorem 5.1, since maps 𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 defined
       as 𝜆𝑔 (ℎ) = 𝑔◦ℎ − 𝑔 in brace 𝐴 have an analogous matrix form as maps
       𝜆𝑃 , 𝜆𝑄 , 𝜆𝑅 , 𝜆𝑆 from 𝐵′ to 𝐵′ in Theorem 5.1. It also follows by a direct
       calculation.
   (2) Let 𝑎 = 𝛼𝑅 + 𝛽𝑄 + 𝛾𝑃 + 𝜉𝑆 for some 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾, 𝜉 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 . Notice that
       𝑄, 𝑃, 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴2 , by the Multiplicative Table. Consider the element 𝑎1 =
       𝑅𝑝−𝛼 ◦𝑎. It follows that 𝑎1 = −𝛼𝑅 + 𝑎 + 𝑐 for 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴2 (by the formula
       (𝑑◦𝑏) ∗ 𝑎 = 𝑑 ∗ 𝑎 + 𝑑 ∗ (𝑏 ∗ 𝑎) + 𝑏 ∗ 𝑎 applied several times). Notice
       that since 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴2 it follows that 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 as otherwise 𝐴 = 𝐴2 ,
       hence 𝐴 = 𝐴2 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴3 , so 𝐴 = 𝐴5 = 0. Consequently,
       𝐴2 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝔽𝑝 𝑆. Therefore,
                              𝑎1 = 𝛽 ′ 𝑄 + 𝛾′ 𝑃 + 𝜉 ′ 𝑆,
       for some 𝛽 ′ , 𝛾′ , 𝜉 ′ ∈ 𝔽𝑝 .
                                               ′
          Consider the element 𝑎2 = 𝑄𝑝−𝛽 ◦𝑎1 . It follows that 𝑎2 ∈ −𝛽 ′ 𝑄 +
       𝑎1 + 𝐴3 + 𝐴 ∗ 𝑎1 ⊆ 𝐴3 (since 𝑃, 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴3 and 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴3 ). Notice
       that 𝑃, 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴3 , hence 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴3 as otherwise 𝐴2 = 𝐴3 = 𝐴4 = 𝐴5 = 0.
       Therefore, 𝑎2 = 𝛾′′ 𝑃 + 𝜉 ′′ 𝑆 for some 𝛾′′ , 𝜉 ′′ ∈ 𝔽𝑝 . By the Multiplicative
                                                                          ′′   ′′
       Table 𝑃 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑆 = 0, so 𝑎2 = 𝑃𝛾 ◦𝑆 𝜉 , and
                                      ′ ′′  ′′
       consequently 𝑎 = 𝑅𝛼 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛾 ◦𝑆 𝜉 . This concludes the proof.
   (3) Let 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 . By item 2 above we can write 𝑎 = 𝑅𝛼 ◦𝑄𝛽 ◦𝑃𝛾 ◦𝑆 𝜉 for
       some 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾, 𝜉 ≤ 𝑝. Then
                   𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑏 = 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝜆𝑅𝛼 (𝜆𝑄𝛽 (𝜆𝑃𝛾 (𝜆𝑆𝜉 (𝑏))),
       and it can be calculated using the Multiplicative Table to give a concrete
       element from 𝔽𝑝 𝑅+𝔽𝑝 𝑄+𝔽𝑝 𝑃+𝔽𝑝 𝑆. This determines uniquely a brace
       (𝐴, +, ◦).
   (4) Consider the subgroup 𝐴′ of (𝐴, ◦) generated by elements 𝑅, 𝑄, 𝑃, 𝑆.
       Then by item 2 above, we have that 𝐴′ has cardinality 𝑝4 , so 𝐴′ = (𝐴, ◦).
514              D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

          By item 1 above, 𝐴′ satisfies all the relations of group XV, which con-
          cludes the proof (since 𝐴′ has the same cardinality as group XV).
                                                                     −1
      (5) Observe that by Multiplicative Table we obtain (𝑆 ∗ 𝑄) ∗ ( 𝑅) = 𝑆, so
                                                                        𝑦
         𝐴 cannot be right nilpotent.
                                                                                  
Theorem 6.3. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) an 𝔽𝑝 -brace which is
not right nilpotent with multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) being the group XV. Then the
𝔽𝑝 -brace 𝐴 is isomorphic to some brace constructed in Theorem 5.5.
Proof. Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace which is not right nilpotent with multi-
plicative group (𝐴, ◦) being the group XV. Then (𝐴, +, ◦) satisfies the relations
from the Multiplicative Table by Proposition 4.15 for some 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 , 𝑦 ≠ 0.
   Let 𝐵 be the brace constructed in Theorem 5.5 for the same 𝑖, 𝑘, 𝑦. Then 𝐵
satisfies the same Multiplicative Table as 𝐴, by Theorem 6.1. By Theorem 6.2,
item 3, braces which satisfy the same Multiplicative Table coincide, so 𝐴 and 𝐵
are isomorphic braces.                                                         

7. Some properties of the constructed braces
   Recall that a brace is called prime if product of any two non-zero ideals in
this brace is non-zero.
Proposition 7.1. Let 𝑝 > 3 be a prime number. Let 𝐴 be a brace constructed in
Theorem 5.5 for fixed 𝑦, 𝑖, 𝑘 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑦 ≠ 0. Then 𝐴 is a prime brace. Moreover,
𝐴 contains a non-zero strongly nilpotent (i.e., both right and left nilpotent) ideal
𝐴2 .
Proof. A non-zero ideal 𝐼 in 𝐴 contains a non-zero element 𝑐 = 𝛼1 𝑅 + 𝛼2 𝑄 +
𝛼3 𝑃 + 𝛼4 𝑆 for some 𝛼1 , 𝛼2 , 𝛼3 , 𝛼4 ∈ 𝔽𝑝 . If 𝑐 ∉ 𝐴4 , then when multiplying 𝑐
from the left several times by either 𝑅 or 𝑄 we obtain some non-zero element
in 𝐴4 , hence 𝐼 contains 𝑆 ∈ 𝐴4 . Since every ideal containing 𝑆 contains 𝑄, 𝑃
we get that 𝐴2 ⊆ 𝐼 (since 𝑆 ∗ 𝑄 = −𝑃, 𝑆 ∗ 𝑅 = −𝑄 + 𝑃 − 2−1 𝑦𝑆). Notice that
𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 ≠ 0 since 𝑄 ∗ 𝑄 ≠ 0, so 𝐴 is a prime brace, as every product of non-
zero ideals in 𝐴 is non-zero. Moreover, (𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 ) ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴2 ∗ (𝐴2 ∗ 𝐴2 ) = 0,
so 𝐴2 is a strongly nilpotent ideal in 𝐴.                                      
Example 7.2. Consider a vector space 𝑉 spanned by the elements 𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆 over
the field 𝔽𝑝 with 𝑝 elements, with multiplication that satisfies
                    (𝑎 + 𝑏)𝑐 = 𝑎𝑐 + 𝑏𝑐 and 𝑎(𝑏 + 𝑐) = 𝑎𝑏 + 𝑎𝑐
for all 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 in 𝑉. Furthermore, the following relations hold in 𝑉.
      𝑃𝑆 = 𝑆𝑆 = 𝑄𝑆 = 𝑅𝑆 = 𝑃𝑃 = 𝑆𝑃 = 𝑄𝑃 = 𝑃𝑄 = 𝑅𝑄 = 𝑄𝑅 = 0,
      𝑅𝑅 = 𝑗𝑃 + 𝑘𝑆, 𝑄𝑄 = −𝑦𝑆, 𝑅𝑃 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑆𝑄 = −𝑃, 𝑃𝑅 = 𝑦𝑆, 𝑆𝑅 = −𝑄,
where 𝑗, 𝑘, and non-zero 𝑦 are arbitrary elements from 𝔽𝑝 . Now, it is easily checked
that this defines a pre-Lie algebra by verifying that
                       (𝐴𝐵)𝐶 − 𝐴(𝐵𝐶) = (𝐵𝐴)𝐶 − 𝐵(𝐴𝐶)
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS           515

is satisfied for any 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶 ∈ {𝑃, 𝑄, 𝑅, 𝑆}. Hence 𝑉 is an example of a pre-Lie
algebra which is left nilpotent and not right nilpotent.
   The relations in 𝑉 were obtained using the formula found in [20] for obtain-
ing a pre-Lie algebra from a strongly nilpotent 𝔽𝑝 -brace to the brace defined in
Theorem 5.5, and some relations were guessed as to avoid large calculations.

8. Braces whose multiplicative group is XIV
  In this section, we will show that all 𝔽𝑝 -braces whose multiplicative group is
XIV are right nilpotent and strongly nilpotent provided that 𝑝 is a prime num-
ber larger than 3. Recall that 𝔽𝑝 is the field of cardinality 𝑝.

Lemma 8.1. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Let 𝑖 be such that 𝐴𝑖+1 = 0 and suppose there is 0 ≠ 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴𝑖 such that
𝑐◦𝑎 = 𝑎◦𝑐 for all 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴. Then 𝐴 is a right nilpotent brace.
Proof. Observe that 𝑐 ∗ 𝑐 = 0 hence 𝑐𝑗 = 𝑗𝑐 for 𝑗 = 1, 2, … , 𝑝. Denote 𝔽𝑝 𝑐 =
{𝑐𝑗 ∶ 𝑗 = 1, 2, … , 𝑝} by 𝐼. Then 𝐼 is an ideal in brace 𝐴, and 𝐼 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐼 = 0,
since 𝐼 = {𝑐𝑗 ∶ 𝑗 = 1, 2, … , 𝑝} and 𝑐𝑗 is a central element in 𝐴 for every 𝑗 (recall
that 𝑐𝑗 = 𝑐◦ ⋯ ◦𝑐). Notice that 𝐴∕𝐼 has cardinality not exceeding 𝑝3 , hence
𝐴∕𝐼 is a right nilpotent brace by [2]. Now 𝐴 ∗ 𝐼 = 0 yields that 𝐴 is a right
nilpotent brace.                                                                   
Lemma 8.2. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Suppose that the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XIV. Denote by
𝑊 = {𝑃𝑖 ◦𝑄𝑗 ∶ 𝑖, 𝑗 = 1, 2, … , 𝑝}. Suppose that 𝐴 is not a right nilpotent brace.
Then the following holds.
   (1) 𝐴3 ≠ 0.
   (2) Suppose that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 . If 𝐴4 = 0 and 𝐴3 ≠ 0, then the cardinality of 𝐴2 is
       𝑝3 and 𝐴2 = 𝑊 + 𝐴3 . Moreover 𝐴3 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0.
   (3) Suppose that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 . If 𝐴5 = 0 and 𝐴4 ≠ 0, then the cardinality of 𝐴2 is
       𝑝3 and 𝐴2 = 𝑊 + 𝐴4 . Moreover, 𝐴4 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0.
Proof.       (1) follows from Lemma 8.1, since 𝑃 = 𝑅−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑅◦𝑆 ∈ 𝐴2 by
        Lemma 4.4 and 𝑃 is a central element in (𝐴, ◦).
    (2) Notice that since 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝑊 ⊆ 𝐴2 . By Lemma 8.1, we have
        𝑊 ∩ 𝐴3 = 0, since 𝑊 consists of central elements. Therefore, 𝑊 +
        𝐴3 , 𝐴3 ◦𝑊 ⊆ 𝐴2 , and since 𝐴2 ≠ 𝐴 and 𝑊 + 𝐴3 has cardinality 𝑝3 , it
        follows that 𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝3 and 𝐴2 = 𝑊 + 𝐴3 = 𝐴3 ◦𝑊.
           Observe now that
     𝐴3 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴3 ∗ (𝑊 + 𝐴3 ) = 𝐴3 ∗ 𝑊 + 𝐴3 ∗ 𝐴3 = 𝑊 ∗ 𝐴3 ⊆ 𝐴4 = 0.
    (3) Notice that since 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 , then 𝑊 ⊆ 𝐴2 . By Lemma 8.1, we have
        𝑊 ∩ 𝐴4 = 0, since 𝑊 consists of central elements. Therefore, 𝑊 +
        𝐴4 , 𝐴4 ◦𝑊 ⊆ 𝐴2 , and since 𝐴2 ≠ 𝐴 and 𝑊 + 𝐴4 has cardinality 𝑝3 , it
        follows that 𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝3 and 𝐴2 = 𝑊 + 𝐴4 = 𝐴4 ◦𝑊.
516              D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

             Observe now that
       𝐴4 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴4 ∗ (𝑊 + 𝐴4 ) = 𝐴4 ∗ 𝑊 + 𝐴4 ∗ 𝐴4 = 𝑊 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0.
                                                                             
Lemma 8.3. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Suppose that the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XIV. Suppose
that 𝐴 is not a right nilpotent brace. Suppose that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 and 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 . Then
𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 0.
Proof. Notice that 𝐴∕𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝, by Lemma 8.2. Therefore, 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 ∈
𝐴2 for some 𝑖, since 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 . Let 𝑊 be as in Lemma 8.2. By Lemma 8.2, we have
𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 = 𝑐◦𝑤 for some 𝑤 ∈ 𝑊 and some 𝑐 ∈ 𝐴𝑖 where 𝐴𝑖+1 = 0. Therefore,
𝑆 ′ = 𝑆◦𝑅𝑖 ◦𝑤−1 ∈ 𝐴𝑖 (where 𝐴𝑖+1 = 0). Recall that 𝑤 is a central element, so
𝑅◦𝑆 ′ = 𝑆 ′ ◦𝑅◦𝑃. This implies that
                  0 = 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑆 ′ ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑃) + 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃.
Notice that 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝐴2 = 0 by Lemma 8.2, so 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑅 + 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃 = 0.
   Observe now that (𝑅◦𝑆 ′ ) ∗ 𝑅 = (𝑆 ′ ◦𝑅◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑅. Therefore, 𝑅 ∗ (𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑅) =
𝑅 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑅) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅, since 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝐴2 = 0. Substituting 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑅 = −(𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃)
in the left hand side we get 𝑅 ∗ (𝑅 ∗ 𝑃) + 𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, so 𝜆𝑅 (𝑅 ∗ 𝑃) = 0, hence
𝑅 ∗ 𝑃 = 0, as the map 𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝑎 ∗ 𝑏 + 𝑏 is an invertible map in any brace. 
Lemma 8.4. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Suppose that the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XIV. Suppose
that 𝐴 is not right nilpotent. Suppose that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 and 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 . Then 𝑆 ∉ 𝐴2 and
𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0.
Proof. Notice that 𝑆 ∉ 𝐴2 as otherwise (𝐴, ◦) would be generated by elements
from 𝐴2 implying 𝐴 = 𝐴2 , which is impossible as then
                     𝐴 = 𝐴2 = 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴2 = 𝐴3 = 𝐴4 = 𝐴5 = 0.
      Notice that 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 implies that 𝑅 = 𝑎◦𝑤 for some 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴𝑖 , 𝑤 ∈ 𝑊, where
𝐴𝑖+1 = 0, by Lemma 8.2. Therefore, 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑤−1 ∈ 𝐴𝑖 . Notice that since 𝑤 is
central in the group (𝐴, ◦), we get 𝑅′ ◦𝑆 = 𝑆◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃. Consequently, 𝑅′ ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗
𝑃 + 𝑃 since 𝐴 ∗ 𝑅′ = 0 and 𝑅′ ∗ 𝑃 ⊆ 𝑅′ ∗ 𝐴2 = 0 by Lemma 8.2.
  Observe now that (𝑅′ ◦𝑆) ∗ 𝑆 = (𝑆◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑆, hence
𝑅′ ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑆) = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅′ ∗ 𝑆)+𝑆 ∗ (𝑅′ ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑆))+𝑆 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑆)+𝑅′ ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑆)+𝑃 ∗ 𝑆.
Recall that 𝑅′ ∗ 𝐴2 = 0 and 𝐴 ∗ 𝑅′ = 0 by Lemma 8.2; consequently,
                      0 = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑅′ ∗ 𝑆) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑆).
Substituting 𝑅′ ∗ 𝑆 = 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃 in the right hand side we get
                    0 = 𝑆 ∗ (𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 + 𝑃) + 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 + 𝑆 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑆),
therefore 2𝜆𝑆 (𝑆 ∗ 𝑃) = 0, so 𝑆 ∗ 𝑃 = 0.                                     
      SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS          517

Proposition 8.5. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Suppose that the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group XIV. Suppose
that 𝐴 is not a right nilpotent brace. Then 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴2 .

Proof. Suppose on the contrary that 𝑄 ∈ 𝐴2 . If 𝑅 ∉ 𝐴2 , then 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 0
by Lemma 8.3. Observe that 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝐴2 , since 𝐴∕𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝, by
Lemma 8.2. Observe now that for 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐴 we have (𝑃◦𝑥) ∗ 𝑦 = (𝑥◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑦,
and by Lemma 4.4 we get

             𝑃 ∗ (𝑥 ∗ 𝑦) = 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑦) ⊆ 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑅 + 𝐴2 ))
                           = 𝑥 ∗ 𝑃 ∗ (𝐴2 ) ⊆ 𝑥 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0

(since 𝑃 = 𝑅−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑅◦𝑆 is in group 𝑋𝐼𝑉). Consequently, 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0, and
since 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅 = 0, then 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 0. Since 𝑃 is a central element, we get that
𝐼 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 is an ideal in 𝐴. By [2], every brace of cardinality not exceeding 𝑝3 is
right nilpotent, hence 𝐴∕𝐼 is right nilpotent. Now 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 yields that 𝐴 is
right nilpotent.
   Suppose now that 𝑅 ∈ 𝐴2 . Then by Lemma 8.4 we have that 𝑆 ∉ 𝐴2 , 𝑆 ∗
𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 0. Observe that 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑆 + 𝐴2 , since 𝐴∕𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝, by
Lemma 8.2. Observe now that for 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐴 we have (𝑃◦𝑥) ∗ 𝑦 = (𝑥◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑦,
and by Lemma 4.4 we get

             𝑃 ∗ (𝑥 ∗ 𝑦) = 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑦) ⊆ 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑆 + 𝐴2 ))
                           = 𝑥 ∗ 𝑃 ∗ (𝐴2 ) ⊆ 𝑥 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0

(since 𝑃 = 𝑅−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑅◦𝑆 is in group XIV). Consequently, 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 = 0, and
since 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 = 0, then 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 0. Since 𝑃 is a central element, we get that
𝐼 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 is an ideal in 𝐴. By [2] every brace of cardinality not exceeding 𝑝2 is
right nilpotent, hence 𝐴 ∗ 𝑅 is right nilpotent. Now 𝐴 ∗ 𝑃 = 0 yields that 𝐴 is
right nilpotent.                                                              

Proposition 8.6. Let 𝐴 be an 𝔽𝑝 -brace of cardinality 𝑝4 , where 𝑝 > 3 is a prime
number. Suppose that the multiplicative group (𝐴, ◦) is the group 𝑋𝐼𝑉. Suppose
that 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴2 . Then 𝐴 is a right nilpotent brace.

Proof. Notice that 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴2 by Lemma 4.4, since 𝑃 = 𝑅−1 ◦𝑆 −1 ◦𝑅◦𝑆 in the group
XIV. By Lemma 8.2 we have that 𝐴∕𝐴2 has cardinality 𝑝, so 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ∈ 𝐴2 , 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ∈
𝐴2 , for some 𝑖, 𝑗, since 𝑄 ∉ 𝐴2 . We have now the following cases.
   Case 1. 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴3 , 𝐴4 ≠ 0. Notice that this implies that 𝐴2 ∕𝐴3 has cardinality
𝑝, and so there are 𝑘, 𝑙 such that 𝑆 ′ = 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ◦𝑃𝑘 ∈ 𝐴3 and 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑙 ∈ 𝐴3 .
Notice that since 𝑄, 𝑃 are central elements we get 𝑃 = 𝑅′−1 ◦𝑆 ′−1 ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ , hence
by Lemma 4.4 we have 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 . By Lemma 8.1 we find that 𝐴 is right nilpotent.
   Case 2. 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴3 , 𝐴4 = 0. Denote by 𝑆 ′ = 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ∈ 𝐴2 , 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ∈
𝐴 . We know that 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ ∈ 𝐴2 . Notice that since 𝑄 is central we get 𝑃 =
  2

𝑅′−1 ◦𝑆 ′−1 ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ , hence by Lemma 4.4 we have 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 . By Lemma 8.1 we
find that 𝐴 is right nilpotent.
518             D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

   Case 3. 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴3 . Notice that 𝐴4 ≠ 0 and 𝑃 ∉ 𝐴4 by Lemma 8.2 since 𝑃 is
central. By Corollary 4.2 we have 𝐴𝑖 ∕𝐴𝑖+1 has cardinality 𝑝 for 𝑖 = 1, 2, 3, 4.
Therefore, 𝐴3 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 and 𝐴 = 𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝐴2 .
   Suppose that there are 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ such that 𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ = 𝑆 ′ ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃, and either 𝑆 ′ ∈
𝐴 , 𝑅′ ∈ 𝐴4 or 𝑆 ′ ∈ 𝐴4 and 𝑅′ ∈ 𝐴2 . We will show that 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0.
  2

   Suppose first that 𝑆 ′ ∈ 𝐴4 and 𝑅′ ∈ 𝐴2 . Observe that

                          (𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ ) ∗ 𝑄 = (𝑆 ′ ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑄,

hence 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0, because 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 ′ ∈ 𝐴5 = 0,

                      𝐴 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑄) ⊆ 𝐴 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑃) ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0,

 𝑆 ′ ∗ (𝑅′ ∗ 𝑄) = 𝑆 ′ ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑅′ ) ⊆ 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝐴3 = 𝑆 ′ ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 ) = 𝔽𝑝 (𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑃) = 0,

since 𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝑆 ′ ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0.
   Suppose now that 𝑆 ′ ∈ 𝐴2 and 𝑅′ ∈ 𝐴4 . Observe that (𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ ) ∗ 𝑄 =
(𝑆 ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑄, hence 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0 since 𝑅′ ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑄 ∗ 𝑅′ ∈ 𝐴5 = 0,
  ′


                 𝐴 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑄) ⊆ 𝐴 ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑃) ⊆ 𝐴 ∗ 𝐴4 ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0,

𝑅′ ∗ (𝑆 ′ ∗ 𝑄) = 𝑅′ ∗ (𝑄 ∗ 𝑆 ′ ) ⊆ 𝑅′ ∗ 𝐴3 = 𝑅′ ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑃 + 𝐴4 ) = 𝔽𝑝 (𝑅′ ∗ 𝑃) = 0,

since 𝑅′ ∗ 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ 𝑅′ ⊆ 𝐴5 = 0.
   We will now show that 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 0 implies that 𝐴 is a right nilpotent brace.
Observe that 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴 = 𝑃 ∗ (𝐹𝑝 𝑄 + 𝐴2 ) = 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 , so we need to show that 𝑃 ∗
𝐴2 = 0. Notice that (𝑃◦𝑥) ∗ 𝑦 = (𝑥◦𝑃) ∗ 𝑦 since 𝑃 is central. Consequently,

             𝑃 ∗ (𝑥 ∗ 𝑦) = 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑦) = 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ (𝔽𝑝 𝑄 + 𝐴2 ))
                            = 𝔽𝑝 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ 𝑄) + 𝑥 ∗ (𝑃 ∗ (𝐴2 )) = 0,

since 𝑃 ∗ 𝐴2 ⊆ 𝐴4 by Corollary 4.6, and 𝑃 ∗ 𝑄 = 𝑄 ∗ 𝑃 ∈ 𝐴4 .
   We will now show that it is possible to find such 𝑅′ , 𝑆 ′ . We know that 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗
and 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 are both in 𝐴2 . Suppose that 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ∈ 𝐴3 . Then 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑘 ∈ 𝐴4 for
some 𝑘, and we can take 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ◦𝑃𝑘 and 𝑆 ′ = 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 (since 𝑃, 𝑄 are central).
If 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ∈ 𝐴3 , then 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ◦𝑃𝑘 ∈ 𝐴4 for some 𝑘, and we can take 𝑆 ′ = 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 ◦𝑃𝑘
and 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 .
   If 𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 , 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 ∉ 𝐴3 , then (𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 )◦(𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 )𝑡 ∈ 𝐴3 for some 𝑡, and then

                             (𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 )◦(𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 )𝑡 ◦𝑃𝑘 ∈ 𝐴4

for some 𝑘. Therefore, we can take 𝑆 ′ = (𝑆◦𝑄𝑖 )◦(𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 )𝑡 ◦𝑃𝑘 and 𝑅′ = 𝑅◦𝑄𝑗 .
Observe that 𝑅′ ◦𝑆 ′ = 𝑆 ′ ◦𝑅′ ◦𝑃, as required.                           

Corollary 8.7. Let 𝐴 is an 𝔽𝑝 -brace for a prime number 𝑝 > 3. If the multiplica-
tive group of 𝐴 is isomorphic to the group XIV, then 𝐴 is right nilpotent.
       SOME BRACES OF CARDINALITY 𝑝4 AND RELATED HOPF-GALOIS EXTENSIONS           519

9. Conclusions and applications
   In this section, we give some motivation for constructing concrete example of
braces of a given cardinality. Two main applications of braces are set-theoretic
solutions and Hopf-Galois extensions. The connection between braces and
Hopf-Galois extensions was first observed by David Bachiller in [3]. This topic
was subsequently investigated in [21], [12] and many other papers by Truman,
Kohl, Byott, Childs and others. The following exposition follows the above lit-
erature on the topic.
9.1. Hopf-Galois extensions corresponding to a brace. All Hopf-Galois
structures of type (𝐴, +) arise as regular subgroups of Hol(𝐴, +), cf. [3, 2, 12, 13]
for relevant definitions and further details. Now for each brace (𝐴, +, ◦) we
have that (𝐴, ◦) embeds in Hol(𝐴, +) as a regular subgroup through the map
                     𝑚 ∶ (𝐴, ◦) ⟶ Hol(𝐴, +), 𝑎 ⟼ 𝑎𝜆𝑎 .
Isomorphic braces correspond to regular subgroups which are conjugate by an
element of Aut(𝐴, +) inside Hol(𝐴, +). On the other hand, each regular sub-
group 𝐺 ⊂ Hol(𝐴, +) gives a bijection
                         𝜓 ∶ 𝐺 ⟶ (𝐴, +), 𝑔 ⟼ 𝑔(0),
through which we can define a multiplication on (𝐴, +) by
                                 (                )
                         𝑎◦𝑏 = 𝜓 𝜓 −1 (𝑎)𝜓 −1 (𝑏)
which yields a brace (𝐴, +, ◦).
  Therefore, given a brace (𝐴, +, ◦) and an automorphism 𝛾 ∈ Aut(𝐴, +), we
can create, another isomorphic brace (𝐴, +, ◦𝛾 ) by embedding
                         𝑚
               (𝐴, ◦)         𝐺 ⊂ Hol (𝐴, +)

                                     ≀ 𝐶𝛾

                                                 𝜓
                                𝐺𝛾 = 𝛾𝐺𝛾−1              (𝐴, +).

The new circle operation is through
                                      (               )
                             𝑎◦𝛾 𝑏 = 𝜓 𝜓−1 (𝑎)𝜓−1 (𝑏)
in terms of holomorph. This corresponds to defining
                              𝑎◦𝛾 𝑏 = 𝛾−1 (𝛾(𝑎)◦𝛾(𝑏))
as in this case (𝐴, +, ◦) and (𝐴, +, ◦𝛾 ) are isomorphic as braces, so they corre-
spond to regular subgroups inside holomorph which are conjugate by 𝛾.
   Now if 𝛾 ∈ Aut(𝐴, +, ◦), then (𝐴, +, ◦) and (𝐴, +, ◦𝛾 ) are the same and
that means 𝐺𝛾 = 𝐺 inside the holomorph. For a brace (𝐴, +, ◦) and for each
coset representative 𝛾 ∈ Aut(𝐴, +)∕Aut(𝐴, +, ◦), we find a distinct Hopf-Galois
structure (𝐴, +, ◦𝛾 ). As we move through the braces with additive group (𝐴, +),
we get all the Hopf-Galois structures of type (𝐴, +).
520                D. PULJIĆ, A. SMOKTUNOWICZ AND K. NEJABATI ZENOUZ

  Therefore, we can summarise on how to construct Hopf-Galois extensions
corresponding to a given brace as follows:
    (1) Let (𝐴, +, ◦) be a brace.
    (2) Let 𝛾𝑖 be the automorphisms of the abelian group (𝐴, +).
    (3) Check which 𝛾𝑖 are also automorphisms of the whole brace (𝐴, +, ◦).
    (4) We find coset representatives of Aut(𝐴, +)∕Aut(𝐴, +, ◦) and call them
        𝜉1 , 𝜉2 , …. Recall that 𝛼 and 𝛽 are the same in Aut(𝐴, +)∕Aut(𝐴, +, ◦) iff
        𝛼 = 𝛽𝛾 for some 𝛾 ∈ Aut(𝐴, +, ◦) (so 𝛼(𝑎) = 𝛽(𝛾(𝑎)) for all 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴).
    (5) For the automorphisms 𝜉𝑖 of the group (𝐴, +) from our list above we
        find the brace (𝐴𝜉𝑖 , +, ◦𝜉𝑖 ), with the same set 𝐴𝜉𝑖 as the set 𝐴 and with
        the same addition and with the multiplication
                               𝑎◦𝜉𝑖 𝑏 = 𝜉𝑖−1 (𝜉𝑖 (𝑎)◦𝜉𝑖 (𝑏)).
      (6) For the brace 𝐴𝜉𝑖 the corresponding Hopf-Galois extension is the regu-
          lar subgroup (𝑎, 𝜆𝑎 ) (denoted above as 𝑎𝜆𝑎 ) of the holomorph Hol(𝐴, +)
          where
                                  𝜆𝑎 (𝑏) = 𝑎◦𝜉𝑖 𝑏 − 𝑎.
Since we now know how to construct Hopf-Galois extensions corresponding to
the given brace, we can now obtain all Hopf-Galois extensions of type (𝐴, +)
with Galois group 𝐺. Following the beginning of this chapter, it can be sum-
marised in the following way.
    (1) Find all non-isomorphic braces (𝐵, +, ◦) whose additive group (𝐵, +) is
         isomorphic to the group (𝐴, +) and whose multiplicative group (𝐵, ◦) is
         isomorphic to 𝐺.
    (2) We list these non-isomorphic braces as 𝐵1 , 𝐵2 , …. All these braces have
         the same additive group, which is isomorphic to (𝐴, +), and the same
         multiplicative group, which is isomorphic to 𝐺.
    (3) For each brace 𝐵𝑖 from our list we will construct corresponding Hopf-
         Galois extensions.
    (4) To get all Hopf-Galois extensions of type (𝐴, +) with Galois group 𝐺
         we need to collect all the Hopf-Galois extensions constructed for every
         brace 𝐵𝑖 . All these Hopf-Galois extensions are distinct.
The above reasoning can be applied to any brace, so in particular can be applied
to all braces constructed in our paper. This would involve some calculations
to characterise automorphisms of the constructed braces, so we omitted the
calculations and only explained the main ideas in this chapter.
